Overview
Injuries to the cervical spine in athletes may be severe and may be associated with a risk of
permanent neurologic damage.
Various injuries to the cervical spine can occur in athletes, including cervical strain, cervical
disk herniation, transient brachial plexus neurapraxia, transient quadriparesis, spinal canal
stenosis, cervical spine fracture, or spinal cord injury (SCI).
Although cervical spine injuries are most common in contact sports, they also may occur in
non-contact sports.
Some cervical spine injuries may be career-ending; however, other cervical spine injuries may
permit an athlete to return to play (RTP) if the risk of reinjury is minimized.
Epidemiology
Sports are the fourth most common cause of SCI and the second most common cause of SCI in
individuals younger than 30 years.1
Cervical spine injuries are most common in contact sports, such as football or rugby, and in
diving, skiing, cycling, and horseback riding; however, they also occur in non-contact sports.2-9
Injuries to the cervical spine occur more frequently in competition than in practice.10-12
In a study of football players, the most common cervical spine injury sustained was a stinger,
followed by a cervical strain.10
Cervical spine injuries may have a substantial effect on the careers of professional athletes.13-
15
Rates of cervical spine injury in football have been reduced by rule changes aimed at
discouraging the most common mechanisms of injury (such as spear tackling).16-18
Different anatomic and biomechanical factors are present in children; these factors may
influence their injury susceptibility. Therefore, more than one-half of the vertebral injuries that
occur in children are in the cervical spine.19

Acute cervical spine injuries occur during various sports, including American football,
rugby, wrestling, hockey, recreational diving, horseback riding, skiing, and

competition than during practice.10-12
In a systematic review, individual sports with the highest risk of SCI included diving,
skiing, rugby, and horseback riding. SCIs sustained during hockey, skiing, diving, and
American football were almost entirely cervical spine injuries, whereas more than one-
half of horseback riding and snowboarding SCIs were thoracic or lumbosacral spine
injuries.20 Football was the leading cause of cervical sprains in the United States.21
At the high school level, cervical spine injury rates are highest in football, wrestling, and
female gymnastics. Muscle injuries are the most common, followed by nerve injuries.
Compared with other sports, a larger proportion of football injuries were nerve injuries,
and a larger proportion of male ice hockey injuries were cervical spine fractures.22 At the
collegiate level, rates of cervical spine injury are highest in football, male wrestling, male
ice hockey, and female ice hockey. In sex-comparable sports, males are 1.36 times more
likely to suffer a neck or cervical spine injury than females.11
Among collegiate football players, stingers were the most common cervical injury (1.87
per 10,000 athlete-exposures), followed by cervical strains (0.80 per 10,000 athlete-
exposures). Most athletes returned to play within 24 hours of the initial injury (64.4%),
whereas 2.8% of athletes remained did not RTP for more than 21 days.10 Cervical spine
injuries may have a substantial long-term effect on professional athletes. Among
athletes at the National Football League (NFL) Combine, football players with a history of
cervical spine injury were less likely to be drafted.13 Of NFL players who sustained a
cervical disk herniation, at least 28% were unable to RTP.14 NFL players missed a mean
of 120 days for a cervical spine fracture and a mean of 85 days for a herniated disk.14
These injuries are not uncommon in the NFL, in which spinal injuries account for 7% of
all orthopaedic injuries; of these injuries, cervical spine injuries are the most common.12
The most common mechanism of injury varies by sport. In American football, tackling
produces more cervical spine injuries, whereas blocking produces more lumbar spine
injuries.15 In rugby, most cervical spine injuries occur during scrummage or tackling.23 In
ice hockey players, the most common mechanism of injury is a check from behind, which

found that most serious cervical spine football injuries were caused by axial loading.
Therefore, the National Collegiate Athletic Association and the National Federation of
High School Athletic Associations implemented rule changes to ban spearing and the use
of the top of the helmet to contact an opposing player during a tackle or block. This
resulted in a drastic decrease in cervical spine injuries and quadriplegia between 1976
and 1987 at the high school and collegiate levels.16-18
The anatomic and biomechanical factors that may influence injury susceptibility in
children are different than those in adults. These anatomic and biomechanical factors
include greater mobility of the spine because of ligamentous laxity, shallow angulations
of the facet joints, immature development of the neck musculature, and incomplete
ossification of the vertebrae. Therefore, 60% to 80% of all pediatric vertebral injuries
occur in the cervical region.19 In a study of 51 patients at a pediatric trauma center,
isolated fractures accounted for most injuries. These were most likely to occur at C6 and
C7, and the most common mechanisms of injury were motor vehicle collisions (53%) and
sports (14%).25
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The cervical spine performs two important functions. First, it supports the head and enables
multidirectional motion of the head; second, it protects the spinal cord and the cervical nerve
roots.26,27
The upper cervical spine consists of the occiput and the first two vertebrae: the atlas (C1) and
the axis (C2). The atlantoaxial complex is responsible for a large portion of cervical rotation.27
The lower cervical spine consists of the C3 through C7 vertebrae and accounts for the
remaining range of motion (ROM) of the cervical spine.27
The vertebra (from C3 to C7) are composed of a body and a neural arch formed by the pedicles
and lamina.
The facet joints project superiorly and inferiorly from each pedicle and are synovial joints.

Each motion segment of the spine consists of two contiguous vertebrae, their interposed

Anterior structures of the cervical spine, including the intervertebral disks and the vertebral

The anulus fibrosus, longitudinal ligaments, ligamentum flavum, facet capsules, supraspinous
ligament, interspinous ligament, and paraspinal muscles resist distraction.27
Shear forces are opposed by paraspinal musculature and ligamentous support. Facet joints

The spinal canal is wider at the upper cervical levels and most narrow at C4 through C7.18

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The cervical spine has two very important functions: supporting the head and facilitating
multidirectional movement and protecting the spinal cord.26,27 The cervical spine can be
divided into two main regions: the upper cervical spine (including the occiput, C1, and
C2), which has unique vertebral anatomy, and the lower cervical spine (C3 through C7).
C1 also is called the atlas. It is a ring with two lateral masses that support the occipital
condyles but has no vertebral body. The atlas facilitates motion in the sagittal plane,
accounting for 40% of all cervical flexion and extension and 5° to 10° of lateral
bending.27 C2, called the axis, has a true vertebral body; the odontoid process, or dens,
projects from this. The transverse atlantal ligament stabilizes the atlantodens
articulation to prevent forward translation of the atlas. The atlantoaxial complex is
responsible for 60% of all cervical rotation.27
In the lower cervical spine (C3 through C7), each vertebra consists of a body and a neural
arch formed by the pedicles and lamina. The facet joints project superiorly and inferiorly
from the base of the pedicle to form interlocking joints. The transverse processes and
the spinous process, which serve as muscle attachment sites, also originate from the
neural arch. The lower cervical spine can be further understood as a series of motion

articulations, which include the facet joints and the intervertebral disk. The intervertebral
disk is a flexible synchondrosis that permits flexibility and absorbs load.
Several of the structures in the cervical spine contribute to stability. Compression is
resisted by the vertebral bodies and the intervertebral disks. The anulus fibrosus,
longitudinal ligaments, ligamentum flavum, facet capsules, supraspinous ligaments, and
interspinous ligaments resist distraction. Shear forces are opposed by paraspinal
musculature and ligamentous support, whereas facet joints restrain forward vertebral
translation.27
The spinal cord runs through the spinal canal, which narrows at the lower cervical levels.
At the level of the atlas, the spinal cord occupies less than one-half the cross-sectional
area of the spinal canal; however, the spinal cord occupies almost 75% of the cross-
sectional area of the spinal canal at lower cervical levels.28 Although the diameter of the
spinal cord is relatively consistent between individuals, the diameter of the spinal canal
may vary.27
Younger children have increased physiologic laxity, vertebrae that are not completely
ossified, and facet joint orientations that predispose them to a higher risk for injury from
shear forces.18
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Mechanical deformation of axons alters membrane permeability, cytosolic calcium
concentration, and local vasospasm. These changes can affect the ability of axons to conduct
signals in a reversible or an irreversible manner, depending on the degree and duration of
tension applied.27,29
For most contact sports, the mechanism of injury to the cervical spine is axial
compression.17,27 Some injuries also thought to result from hyperflexion.18
Less common causes of cervical SCI include ischemia, hemorrhage, and edema.30

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
An elastic and temporary deformation of the axons, such as that observed in patients
with transient neurapraxia of the spinal cord, leads to local changes in membrane
permeability that are not permanent. Conversely, cervical spine injuries that result in
instability may cause spinal cord deformation that is more substantial or prolonged,
which makes these injuries less reversible.
A flexed posture with a compressive load shortens the anterior column while distracting
the posterior column, leading to more instability. In addition, flexion of the neck
straightens the cervical spine and reduces the efficacy of the paraspinal muscles as a
shock absorber17,27,30 (Figure 1).

Risk Factors
Several congenital anomalies increase an individual’s risk for traumatic cervical spine injury.
These include abnormalities of the atlantoaxial complex, such as odontoid hypoplasia, or os
odontoideum. They also include Klippel-Feil syndrome, particularly if this results in fusion of
more than two cervical vertebrae or fusion of the upper cervical spine (Figure 2).
Participation in contact sports, such as football, rugby, ice hockey, or wrestling, increases the
risk of cervical spine injury.11,20-22
Risk also is higher for participants in sports that are associated with possible falls or head-first
impact, such as horseback riding, cycling, gymnastics, or diving.19-21
Improper tackling technique has been associated with cervical spine injury.

Maroon and Bailes31 designed a classification system for cervical spine injuries.
Type 1: permanent spinal cord dysfunction; this includes complete SCI or incomplete lesions,
such as anterior cord syndrome or Brown-Séquard syndrome.
Type 2: transient SCIs; this includes spinal cord neurapraxia.
Type 3: disorders associated with radiologic abnormalities without any neurologic deficits;
examples include spinal stenosis, herniated disks, stable or unstable spine fractures, and

Definitions and Types of Cervical Spine Injuries
Acute Cervical Strain
This may result from overuse or be caused by an acute injury, such as whiplash or a
flexion/extension mechanism of injury.
A cervical strain refers to a muscle injury.
A cervical sprain refers to a ligamentous injury.
Cervical Disk Herniation
Symptoms of acute disk herniation may range from radicular pain to acute onset of transient
or permanent SCI.27,32

Cervical Disk Herniation
Depending on the location of the disk herniation, symptoms may range from radicular
pain to SCI. Symptoms often are accompanied by posterior neck pain and paraspinal
muscle spasm. In addition, referred pain to the arm or scapular area may be present.27
Although C6-7 is the most common level for cervical disk herniation in the general
population, a study of NFL athletes found that disk herniation was most common at C3-4
and C5-6.33 Contact sports may increase the risk of cervical disk herniation; however,
non-contact sports may be protective because of improved dynamic muscular spine
support34 (Figure 3).

Traction injury to the brachial plexus
Cervical nerve root compression in the neuroforamina caused by extreme flexion or


Transient Brachial Plexus Neurapraxia
Transient brachial plexus neurapraxia, also called a stinger or a burner, is a relatively
common sports injury. Among collegiate football players, the incidence during an
individual’s career has been reported to be as high as 49% to 65%.36 In a study of young
rugby players, 33% reported a history of a stinger; 20% of players sustained at least one
stinger during a single season.37 The most commonly affected nerve roots are C5 and
C6.36,38 Symptoms may occur in a classic dermatomal or myotomal distribution or they
may involve multiple distributions, depending on the trunk, division, or cord of the
brachial plexus involved. By definition, the symptoms of a stinger should be unilateral. If
symptoms are bilateral or involve upper and lower extremities, then an alternative
diagnosis should be sought.35
Stingers are graded according to the Seddon and Sunderland classification system.35,36
Grade 1 injuries are characterized by preservation of axonal integrity, transient motor or
sensory loss, and remyelination lasting days to weeks. Grade 2 injuries are associated
with axonal damage and Wallerian degeneration. This peaks approximately 7 days
postinjury, and Schwann cells, endoneurium, perineurium, and epineurium are
preserved. As many as 3 weeks may be necessary before axonal damage is observed via

Transient Quadriparesis
Also called cervical cord neurapraxia
Symptoms may include bilateral upper and lower extremity neurologic symptoms, such as
pain, paresthesia, or weakness.
The most commonly proposed mechanism of injury is a hyperextension injury with axial
loading.34
Torg et al39 described the following classification system for transient quadriparesis:
Grade I: symptoms for less than 15 minutes
Grade II: symptoms for 15 minutes to 24 hours
Grade III: symptoms for more than 24 hours

paresthesia, or decreased coordination.

relative cervical spine stenosis is defined as a spinal canal diameter of 10 to 13 mm.34,41,41

Alternative measurements, such as the mean subaxial cervical space available for the spinal

Spinal Stenosis
Absolute cervical stenosis is defined as a spinal canal diameter of less than 10 mm, and
relative cervical stenosis is defined as a spinal canal diameter of 10 to 13 mm.34,41,42
Cervical spinal canal stenosis also can be defined as a Torg-Pavlov ratio of less than 0.843
(Figure 6). The Torg-Pavlov ratio is calculated by dividing the AP diameter of the spinal
canal by the AP diameter of the vertebral body.35 Although the Torg-Pavlov ratio is highly
sensitive (93%), it is associated with a low positive predictive value (0.2%).35,45 In
addition, it may be less reliable in professional football players, who tend to have larger
vertebral body diameters, and canal measurements may be affected by position and
posture.45,46 In addition, normal spinal canal size observed on lateral radiographs does
not preclude the possibility of functional spinal canal stenosis from causes such as
ligamentous hypertrophy or disk protrusion.42 Therefore, some physicians have
suggested alternative measurements, such as the mean subaxial cervical space available
for the spinal cord44 (Figure 7). This is determined via MRI by subtracting the sagittal
diameter of the spinal cord from the disk-level sagittal diameter of the spinal canal at
levels C3 through C6 and averaging these values.35 Other physicians recommend
assessing for functional spinal stenosis on MRI, which can be observed if the cervical
spine canal is so small that it obliterates the protective cushion of the cerebrospinal fluid
or, in extreme cases, deforms the spinal cord itself.45

Complete paraplegia refers to an SCI with complete loss of function below the waist.
Complete quadriplegia refers to an SCI with complete loss of function below the neck.
Four common types of incomplete SCI syndromes:
Brown-Séquard syndrome
Central cord syndrome
Posterior cord syndrome
Anterior cord syndrome

Spinal Cord Injury
Four main types of incomplete SCI syndromes exist (Table 2). Brown-Séquard syndrome
generally is associated with good outcomes. Often this injury results from
hemitransection of the spinal cord from penetrating trauma. It manifests as ipsilateral
motor, vibratory, and proprioceptive deficits, with contralateral loss of pain and
temperature sensation. Central cord syndrome is associated with fair outcomes. This
often occurs after a hyperextension injury or because of a central cervical disk
herniation. Patients usually have weakness in the hands and upper extremities
bilaterally. Often, lower extremity symptoms and sensory symptoms are less severe.
Posterior cord syndrome also is associated with fair outcomes. This is an uncommon
injury that presents as sensory deficits in vibration and proprioception but with
preserved strength and preserved sensation to light touch and pain. Anterior cord
syndrome typically is associated with poor clinical outcomes. This injury often results
from an anterior spinal artery injury, resulting in ischemia. Patients usually have reduced
pain and temperature sensation and motor weakness.

Physical Examination
The first step in examining the cervical spine is to observe alignment and posture.
Specifically, the examiner should note whether normal cervical lordosis is present and
whether the chin is centered over the sternal notch. The spinous processes should then
be palpated for tenderness, step-off, or gapping. The paraspinal muscles also should be
palpated to assess for muscle spasm or pain. Active ROM in the neck should include
flexion of the chin to the chest, extension so the face becomes parallel with horizontal,
lateral rotation to 60° to 90°, and lateral bending, with the patient able to touch the ear
to the shrugged shoulder. While assessing ROM, the examiner should note the speed of
movement and any pain in addition to the ROM reached.
Next, the examiner should perform a neurologic assessment of the extremities. This
includes assessing dermatomal sensation via pin prick and light touch. Muscle strength
also should be assessed. Deep tendon reflexes should be performed; however,
hyperreflexia typically is a late finding in patients with an SCI and may be absent after an
acute injury. Lastly, distal joint position sense also should be assessed.

pathology. The Spurling test, the distraction test, and the shoulder abduction sign all

CCR and NEXUS Low-Risk Criteria
According to the NEXUS Low-Risk Criteria, cervical spine radiographs are not necessary if
patients meet the following criteria: no midline cervical spine tenderness, no evidence of
intoxication, normal alertness, no focal neurologic deficit, and no painful or distracting
injuries.57
According to the CCR, radiographs of the cervical spine are recommended if any high-
risk features are present, including age older than 65 years, high-risk mechanism of
injury, and paresthesia in the extremities. A high-risk mechanism of injury includes a fall
from a height greater than 1 m or five steps; an axial load to the head, such as with
diving; a high-speed (>100 km/hr) motor vehicle collision, including any with roll-over or
ejection; a motorized recreational vehicle collision, or a bicycle collision. Radiography is
unnecessary in patients without high-risk features or if low-risk features are present in a
patient who is able to rotate the head 45° in each direction. Low-risk features include a
simple rear-end motor vehicle collision (not including those in which the vehicle is
pushed into traffic, is hit by a bus or truck, rolls over, or is hit by a high-speed vehicle),
being in a seated position in the emergency department, being ambulatory at any time, a
delayed onset of neck pain, and the absence of midline cervical spine tenderness.58
Comparison studies suggest that the CCR is associated with better sensitivity and
specificity and results in few radiographs compared with the NEXUS low-risk criteria;59
however, both are acceptable criteria for determining the need for imaging.

Evaluation for acute cervical spine injuries via radiography requires careful attention to

cervical spine radiographs, physicians should note any evidence of soft-tissue swelling,
the height of the vertebral bodies, and the alignment of the vertebral bodies. To aid in
this assessment, physicians should ensure that the anterior spinous line, posterior
spinous line, spinolaminar line, and spinous process line are smooth.

Because of the concern for possible underlying cervical spinal canal stenosis, all patients
with an episode of cervical spinal cord neurapraxia require MRI before RTP. Controversy
exists with regard to the manner in which cervical spinal canal stenosis is best measured
or defined. Good consensus shows that athletes with one episode of transient
quadriplegia may RTP if they are asymptomatic, have a normal neurologic examination,
have full cervical spine ROM, have no changes or ligamentous injury observed on T2-

athlete has relative cervical spine stenosis (10 to 13 mm) or absolute cervical spine
stenosis (<10 mm), controversy exists with regard to the timing of safe RTP.

edema observed on MRI is an absolute contraindication to RTP,34,42 whereas other
physicians feel that relative cervical spine stenosis and the absence of spinal cord edema
or other MRI changes may be considered on a patient-by-patient basis.72 In a study of

canal diameter of less than 10 mm required consideration on a patient-by-patient

Spinal Cord Injury
Methylprednisolone has been used to manage acute SCI, and a 2012 Cochrane review
found that methylprednisolone was the only treatment option that was of some benefit
in patients with an acute SCI.73 However, the Congress of Neurological Surgeons
recommended against the use of methylprednisolone.74,75 This was based on concerns
that methylprednisolone only results in marginal motor function improvements but is
associated with numerous adverse effects, including an increased rate of infection. As a
result, the number of Cervical Spine Research Society members who prescribe
methylprednisolone has decreased over time;76 however, some physicians continue to
prescribe methylprednisolone because of a lack of other options.77
Systemic hypothermia was used to manage an SCI in an NFL player with good results,
which increased interest in the use of hypothermia.79 A case series reported on 20
patients treated via spinal cord cooling; however, confounding treatment options and no
controls were included in the study.80 Unfortunately, protocols for hypothermia are not
well defined.18,78 The American Association of Neurological Surgeons/Congress of
Neurological Surgeons Joint Section on Disorders of the Spine and Peripheral Nerves and
Joint Section on Trauma have stated that insufficient evidence exists to recommend for
or against the use of hypothermia.82

Cervical Spine Fracture
Because cervical spine fractures may take many forms and may be associated with additional
injuries, no single treatment algorithm exists.
Stable cervical spine fractures usually can be managed via immobilization with the use of a
rigid or a semi-rigid cervical collar.34,42 After the patient is pain-free, the collar can be
discontinued, and a rehabilitation program can begin.
If the athlete is pain-free, flexion/extension lateral radiographs should be obtained to assess
for stability before RTP in contact sports.34
Surgical management may be required for unstable fractures, neurologic deficits, injuries to
the posterior ligamentous complex, or fractures that fail to heal via nonsurgical
management.42
Any athlete with a cervical spine fracture should avoid RTP in contact or collision sports until
healing is complete, which typically requires approximately 8 to 10 weeks.34,42
In general, athletes may RTP after a stable fracture if they are pain-free, have a normal
neurologic examination, have full ROM of the neck, and demonstrate bony healing.26
In some patients, a cervical spine fracture may alter biomechanics and be associated with an
increased risk for injury with RTP.42 In these patients, RTP decisions may be controversial and
must be individualized.

Cervical Spine Fracture
Because cervical spine fractures may take many forms and are associated with various
additional injuries, no single treatment algorithm exists. Stable cervical spine fractures
usually can be managed via immobilization with the use of a rigid or semi-rigid cervical
collar.34,42 Any contact/collision athlete with a cervical spine fracture should avoid RTP
until bony healing is complete, which typically requires approximately 8 to 10 weeks.34,42
In athletes who are pain-free with full ROM flexion/extension radiographs should be
obtained to assess for stability before considering RTP in contact sports.34 In general,
athletes may RTP after a stable fracture if they are pain-free, have a normal neurologic
examination, have full ROM of the neck, and demonstrate bony healing.26 Some
examples of stable fractures that may allow for RTP after bony healing include stable
compression fractures of the vertebral body without a sagittal component or
involvement of ligamentous or posterior bony structures, healed stable end-plate
fractures without a sagittal component or involvement of posterior or bony ligamentous
structures, and healed spinous process (clay shoveler) fractures.26
In some patients, a cervical spine fracture may alter biomechanics and be associated
with an increased risk for injury with RTP.42 RTP decisions may be controversial and
must be individualized. Fractures that are relative contraindications to RTP, even after
healing, include stable displaced vertebral body compression fractures without a sagittal
component, healed stable fractures involving the elements of the posterior neural ring,
healed fractures of the C1-C2 complex, and minimally displaced compression fractures.
Absolute contraindications to RTP include vertebral body fractures with a sagittal
component, fractures of the vertebral body with associated posterior arch fractures,
comminuted fractures of the vertebral body with displacement into the spinal canal,
healed displaced fractures that result in facet incongruity, atlantooccipital or atlantoaxial
fusion, dynamic instability, multilevel fusion, or substantially limited cervical ROM.26,65
Surgical management may be required for unstable fractures, neurologic deficits,
posterior ligamentous complex injuries, or fractures for which nonsurgical management
fails.42

Outcomes
Outcomes of cervical spine injuries vary greatly, depending on the type of injury.
Contraindications to RTP include spinal canal stenosis (absolute cut-off is a subject of debate),
spear tackler spine, atlantooccipital or atlantoaxial fusion, odontoid hypoplasia, Klippel-Feil
syndrome involving the upper cervical spine or involving multiple levels, ligamentous instability
observed on flexion/extension radiographs, and multilevel cervical fusion.26,38,41,42,65
In general, before RTP in contact or collision sports, patients should be pain-free,
asymptomatic, and neurologically intact, with full strength and cervical spine ROM26 (Figure

Pearls and Pitfalls
All sports medicine practitioners should be familiar with their EAP and the protective
equipment used in the sports they cover. Proper on-field management of cervical spine
injuries is crucial to achieve the best possible outcome for patients.
The need for imaging studies can be assessed via the CCR or the NEXUS Low-Risk Criteria.
In general, CT is preferred over radiography. MRI may be useful in patients in whom neurologic
or ligamentous injury is suspected.
Imaging studies should be obtained in patients with three or more stingers and in patients
with a stinger and persistent symptoms.
Advanced imaging studies are required in patients in whom transient quadriparesis develops
before considering RTP.
Physicians should be familiar with cervical spine injuries and conditions that are absolute
contraindications to RTP.
